content.summary: Every fifth person over the age of 40 years in Pakistan may be affected by chronic kidney disease, Dr Tazeen Jafar, Head, Section of Nephrology pointed this out at a seminar to mark the first World Kidney Day on March 9, 2006 at the Aga Khan Univeris

media.alt: Kidney disease affects every fifth person in Pakistan

content.text: Every fifth person over the age of 40 years in Pakistan may be affected by chronic kidney disease, Dr Tazeen Jafar, Head, Section of Nephrology pointed this out at a seminar to mark the first World Kidney Day on March 9, 2006 at the Aga Khan Univeristy (AKU) Auditorium.

The seminar was organised by AKU on the inaugural theme of 'Early detection and prevention of chronic kidney disease' as similar events took place all over the world. The well attended seminar was intended to inform primary care physicians, general practitioners and family practice doctors about kidney diseases and their treatment.

The event was significant in the wake of worldwide statistics indicating that deaths claimed by infectious diseases will decline by 3% over the next decade while those by chronic diseases - that already account for 72% of the total global burden of disease in people over 30 - will increase by 17% over the next decade. The first World Kidney Day on March 9, 2006 was an effort jointly launched by the International Society of Nephrology (ISN) and the International Federation of Kidney Foundations (IFKF), to raise awareness about chronic kidney diseases.

Dr Tazeen Jafar also discussed screening strategies and programmes that are best suited for a country like Pakistan in her speech at the seminar. Dr Jaffar Naqvi, Chief Executive of the Kidney Foundation of Pakistan, shared his views about the situation of patients with kidney failure on dialysis in Pakistan, and recounted his experience of the End Stage Renal Failure Registry. He stressed the need for government sponsored haemodialysis projects

Other speakers included Dr Waqar Kashif, Assistant Professor and Consultant Nephrologist at AKU, Dr Arshad Ahmed, Consultant Nephrologist, Dr Iqtidar Ahmed Khan, Professor and Consultant Paediatric Nephrologist, and Dr Raziuddin Bayabani, Assistant Professor and Consultant Urologist at AKU.

A panel discussion followed, in which prominent nephrologists of Karachi including Dr Fazal Akhtar (SIUT), Dr Aasim Ahmed (Kidney Center), Dr Muhammed Azharuddin (AKU), Dr Rauf Mazhar (AKU), Dr. Mansoor Shah (AKU), and the speakers of the seminar participated.

Earlier, Dr David Taylor, Acting Provost AKU, cited the seminar as being part of AKU's mission of taking the lead in organising global public health disease prevention programmes. He expressed hope that this seminar will help create awareness about the screening of people in "high-risk groups" for kidney disease and broadcast the importance of this message to government health officials, general physicians, allied health professionals, individuals and families.

AKU regularly holds such seminars, symposia and events as a part of its social responsibility and commitment to the advancement of health research and education, in order to raise awareness about health and education related issues which are of national importance and interest.
